_authoring_conventions.note: Same conventions as fixtures/cinderella — see fixtures/authoring-notes.md. Original, written for this repository. The places are real; every person, family and event in it is invented.
_authoring_conventions.entry_state_and_exit_state: { <entity_id>: { <column>: <value>, ... }, ... } — one object per touched entity, naming only the core columns this scene asserts.
_authoring_conventions.why_this_fixture_exists: The first road-trip package: a story meant to be heard in a car driving Durham to Pilot Mountain, NC, with each scene set on the stretch of road the listener is on when it plays. It is a hand-made experiment to find out whether the engine's prose works heard aloud and tied to real places — before anything is built for route ingestion, timing or text to speech.
_authoring_conventions.one_location_per_road_segment: Each Location is a stretch of the route, not a room. The characters are in the car the whole time until scene 6; the car's location_id is what moves.
_authoring_conventions.characters_present_includes_the_absent: char_hal and char_june are dead before the story opens. They are listed in characters_present where a beat names them, as fixtures/the-lamp-at-cairn-head does for Innes, so the name reaches the writer with a World Model row behind it.
_authoring_conventions.length_budget_is_audio_time: Budgets are words, sized to about 150 spoken words a minute so each scene finishes before the next landmark. See _route_anchoring for the minutes each one has to fill.
_authoring_conventions.route_facts_to_verify: Drive times, the side of the road the mountain appears on, and the US-52 exit number were written from general knowledge, not from a routing API. Check them against Google Maps before judging the timing. The one that matters most is scene 3's plant: the mountain has to appear on the LEFT driving north on US-52, or the title's promise is false.

_route_anchoring.note: Not read by the engine. The trigger data a road-trip player would need — kept here so the experiment records what the scenes were timed against.
_route_anchoring.route: Durham → I-85 S (joined by I-40 near Hillsborough) → I-40 W at the Greensboro split → Winston-Salem → US-52 N → Pilot Mountain State Park → summit road

facts.statement: Hal's letter, left with his will, asked Jess to drive the Buick to Pilot Mountain once before she sold it, to follow the marks in his atlas, and to take someone with her in the passenger seat.
Jess means to sell the Buick right after this trip; she has already written the listing and a buyer is coming to see it next Saturday.
Theo got his learner's permit last month, but his father won't let him practice anywhere busier than a church parking lot.
The sealed envelope in the glovebox is addressed, in Hal's pencil, not to Jess but to 'Shotgun' — whoever rides in the passenger seat — and is to be opened only when they are parked under 'her'.
Every note Hal pencilled along the route in the atlas is written to the passenger, not the driver — 'Shotgun, count the mill windows; driver keeps her eyes on the road.'
At Greensboro, Hal's note says to stay with 40 through Winston and then turn north, and to 'watch for her on the left.' Theo assumes 'her' means June.

Hal's note at Winston-Salem says the mountain was a landmark travelers steered by, and that the name the Saura people gave it, Jomeokee, is usually translated as 'great guide' or 'pilot' — which is why it is called Pilot Mountain.
Hal asked Jess to come to Pilot Mountain with him every fall for twenty years, and she never once went; she always had something.

The letter inside the envelope says the Buick is not Jess's to sell: Hal has left it to whoever rode shotgun on this drive, and he knew Jess would bring Theo, because there was nobody else she could ask.

Hal proposed to June at the Little Pinnacle overlook in October 1962, after driving her there in his first car; the photograph in the atlas was taken a minute afterward, and the hand June is holding up to the camera is the one with the ring.

scene_cards.dramatic_function: Put two reluctant people in a dead man's car on a road he asked them to drive, and hand the listener a sealed envelope and a question: who is it for?
scene_cards.story_time: a Saturday in mid-October, a little after nine in the morning
required_beats: Jess merges the green Buick onto the interstate heading west out of Durham with Theo slouched in the passenger seat, headphones on, one ear out
Jess tells Theo why they are doing this: Hal's letter asked her to drive the car to Pilot Mountain once before she sold it, following the marks in his atlas, and to bring someone to ride along
Theo asks, not kindly, why he is the someone, and Jess doesn't give him the true answer, which is that there was no one else to ask
Jess mentions that the listing is written and a buyer is coming to see the car next Saturday, and Theo goes quiet at that
Theo lets slip that he got his learner's permit last month and that his father won't let him drive anywhere busier than a church parking lot
Jess tells him to open the glovebox for the atlas, and he finds a sealed envelope on top of it, with Hal's pencil on the front: 'Shotgun — open when you're parked under her'
past Hillsborough, where I-40 comes in from the east and the two roads run as one, Theo puts the envelope back unopened, because Hal said to wait
scene_cards.tone: dry, a little funny, the grief kept out of sight under logistics
invariants: Jess never takes her eyes off the road to read anything; only the passenger reads
no one guesses what is in the envelope
the story never speaks to the listener or tells them what to do on the road

scene_cards.dramatic_function: Let Hal speak for the first time, through the atlas, and let the listener notice who he is speaking to.
scene_cards.story_time: the same morning, about half an hour out of Durham
required_beats: Theo opens the atlas to the North Carolina pages and finds the route drawn in soft pencil, with small notes along it in Hal's cramped hand
the first note is at the Haw River, and Theo reads it aloud: 'Shotgun — count the mill windows. Driver keeps her eyes on the road.'
Theo looks for the mill and can't see it from the bridge; the trees have taken the view, and Jess says the town is just off the highway, the mills still standing in it
the note goes on: June counted the windows every time they drove this way, and never got the same number twice
Jess realizes, and says aloud, that every note she can see on the page is written to the passenger, not the driver
Theo, despite himself, turns the page to see what the next note says
scene_cards.tone: warmer; the first real laugh between them, on June's account
invariants: Hal's notes are quoted exactly as short pencil notes, never as long letters
the mill is not visible from the bridge

scene_cards.dramatic_function: Give the listener the promise the whole drive now leans toward — 'watch for her on the left' — and let a character guess wrong about it.
required_beats: as they come into Greensboro, Theo reads the next note, pencilled where I-40 and I-85 separate: 'Here the roads part. Stay with 40. Through Winston, then turn north. Watch for her on the left.'
Jess keeps the car on 40 as 85 peels away to the southwest
Theo decides 'her' means June — that Hal meant them to watch for something of hers, a house or a church or a grave — and Jess, not sure, doesn't correct him
Theo asks what June was like, and Jess finds she has only small things to offer: a laugh, a green coat, the smell of Juicy Fruit
Theo admits the envelope is bothering him, because it says Shotgun and not Jess, and Hal knew who'd be driving
scene_cards.tone: thoughtful, the two of them talking more easily now, a small ache under it
invariants: nobody says out loud that 'her' might be the mountain
the conversation never turns into a eulogy

scene_cards.dramatic_function: Turn the car toward the mountain and plant, lightly, what the mountain is for.
required_beats: the Winston-Salem skyline comes up beside the highway, and Theo reads Hal's note there: that the city used to smell of tobacco when the wind was right, and that he hauled it here in his twenties

the next note sits beside the US-52 North interchange, and Theo reads it as Jess makes the turn: the mountain they are headed to was the landmark travelers steered by, and the Saura people's name for it, Jomeokee, is usually translated 'great guide', which is why it is called the Pilot
Jess says she's heard Hal tell that a hundred times and never listened to it once
Jess mentions the buyer again, a little too firmly, and Theo asks whether she even wants to sell it; she says it isn't about wanting
scene_cards.tone: brighter, the road opening up; the question of the car sitting in the middle of it
invariants: the Jomeokee translation is given as Hal's note, and as 'usually translated', never as certain fact
Theo reads the notes; Jess drives

scene_cards.dramatic_function: Pay off the title in the landscape itself, at the moment the listener can see it too, and let Jess say the thing she's been driving around.
required_beats: past Rural Hall the land starts lifting, and Theo is still watching the roadside for a house or a church that might be June's
the knob comes up ahead and to the left, alone above the farmland, a bare rock pinnacle with a cap of trees, and Theo says 'oh' — it's her; Hal meant the mountain
Jess admits that Hal asked her to come up here with him every October for twenty years and she never once came; there was always something
Theo doesn't say anything for a while, then says that 'parked under her' must mean the park, and takes the envelope out of the glovebox and holds it on his knee
scene_cards.tone: a held breath; the one moment of real awe in the story, kept plain
invariants: the mountain is described as it is — a bare rock knob topped with trees — and never made mystical
Theo does not open the envelope yet

scene_cards.dramatic_function: Open the envelope, and turn the whole drive over: it was never a trip to get rid of the car. It was a handover.

obj_buick.status: parked at the foot of the summit road

required_beats: Jess takes the exit for Pilot Mountain State Park and follows the road to the lot at the foot of the summit road, and parks, the mountain right above them
Theo opens the envelope and reads Hal's letter aloud: it is written to whoever rode shotgun, exactly as the notes in the atlas were
the letter says the Buick is not Jess's to sell — Hal has left it to whoever sat in that seat today, and he knew it would be Theo, because Jess wouldn't have asked anyone else
Jess understands that the listing and the buyer were never going to happen, and that Hal planned this drive so she'd have company on it whether she wanted it or not
Theo says he can't drive it, he's fifteen; Jess reminds him he has a permit, and she is sitting right here
scene_cards.tone: quiet, then funny, then very nearly tears — Jess's, not Theo's
invariants: Hal's letter is short and plain, in his voice, and never sentimental about itself
Jess does not argue with the letter

scene_cards.dramatic_function: Swap the seats, so the last note in the atlas finds its reader: Jess, riding shotgun for the first time, finally at the place she never came.

obj_photograph.status: hidden between the last two pages of the North Carolina map

required_beats: Theo calls his father on speaker and asks if he can drive the summit road with Jess beside him, and his father, after a long pause, says yes
they change seats; Theo drives the switchbacks slowly and exactly, both hands on the wheel, and Jess, riding shotgun now, opens the atlas on her knees
on the last page of the route, where the pencil line ends at the mountain, there is one more note for the passenger, and a small photograph tucked beside it

the photograph is Hal and June at a stone wall with the bare rock of the Big Pinnacle behind them, June holding her left hand up to the camera; the note says he asked her here, in October 1962, and she said yes before he'd finished asking

they walk out to the Little Pinnacle overlook together, the Big Pinnacle straight across from them and the whole Piedmont they drove across laid out below, and Theo says it makes sense now why they called it the Pilot
Jess stands where the photograph was taken, for the first time, and lets herself cry, and Theo has the decency to look at the view
scene_cards.tone: open, bright, earned; end on the view, not on a speech
invariants: Theo drives carefully and legally, with Jess beside him, and the story never makes a joke of unsafe driving
no one climbs the Big Pinnacle; they look at it from the overlook
the story ends at the overlook, with nothing explained that the listener has already understood

voice_card.narrative_distance: close third on Jess, who notices more than she says
voice_card.register: plain, warm and precise; written to be heard aloud in a moving car, so every sentence must make sense on one hearing
voice_card.sentence_rhythm: mostly short and medium sentences a narrator can say in one breath; no parentheses, no nested clauses, no lists a listener has to hold in their head
imagery_palette: the inside of an old car: bench seat, dash, glovebox
ridges turning blue in the distance
voice_card.dialogue_density: moderate to high; the story is mostly two people talking in a car. Attribute every line so a listener always knows who is speaking — prefer 'Theo said' before or right after the line
voice_card.style_exemplar: Theo read the note twice before he read it out loud. "Shotgun," he said. "Count the mill windows. Driver keeps her eyes on the road." Jess kept her eyes on the road.
voice_card.reader_familiarity: The listener is in a car on this same road, hearing this, not reading it. Name real places plainly, the way a local would. Never describe the page, the text, or anything the listener would have to see.
